TERRACE F. CLUB |

Dear Terrans,

Even as the University grows endlessly in all directions, our
Terrace Club is staying rooted in what we do best.

In the kitchen and on the stage, we still crank up the volume
while staying true to our roots. We’re serving 19 meals a week,
doubling down on creative menus that they never see on Prospect.
And our social calendar remains the envy of the Street. So it’s
no wonder that Terrace continues to draw a crowd, with 133
sophomores choosing us at sign-ins this winter.

Looking ahead, the Board is focused on ensuring the club’s long-
term sustainability. We are taking care of our 1904 house, and
this winter undertook a major project to upgrade our heating
system. Making sure that "Food = Love" has a permanent home takes
work, and so we're actively seeking new volunteers among our base
of committed alumni.

There's something for everyone to do, and there are no
geographical restrictions here in 2026 (I live in California). So
if you're looking for a way to reconnect with Princeton, activate
a community of brilliant people, and secure your favorite home-
away-from-home for another generation, please drop me a note at
steve. feyer@terracefclub.org.

Food to all,
Steve Feyer '03
Chair, Board of Governors

ALUMNI
VISITORS
POLICY

Alumni visitors are not entitled to admission to
the Club and should seek permission from the
Club Manager and/or Undergraduate Officers by
submitting their requests to visit to
visitors@terracefclub.org. Requests should be
submitted at least 72 hours in advance of the
proposed visitation date. The Club Manager
and/or Undergraduate Officers reserve the right
to approve, deny, limit, or rescind visitation
privileges for any legally permissible reason,
before and during the visit, and are not required
to provide an explanation for any decision.

We are grateful for Terrace Governance
Committee Co-Chairs Beverly Nwanna
'09 and Jon Strassfeld '09 for their
leadership in revising the bylaws for the
Terrace Board of Directors.

We thank Mihalis Alisandratos '18, Peter
Baltera 10, Jon Feyer '09, Steve Feyer '03,
Mike Hodgson '04, Jasmine Jeffers 11,
Jenny Korn '96, Suneil Vallabh '09, and
Ari Vera "12 for their feedback on bylaws.
Over several meetings of many hours,
our bylaws are now updated!

All decisions by the Club Manager and/or
Undergraduate Officers are final, and there
shall be no right of appeal to the Board of
Governors or any higher authority. The Club
anager and/or Undergraduate Officers
also reserve the right to take any legally
permissible action necessary to enforce this
policy, or violations thereof, including
involving law enforcement. Exceptions to
his policy, including events such as
Homecoming, Lawn Parties, Alumni Day,
and Reunions, will be communicated to
Terrace alumni in advance.

SR | OST IN TRINBAGO

Le

a

Some years ago—in the era that | like to call “B.C.," or “Before COVID"—my

mother questioned why, come hell or high water, | had always made sure to

make it from my hometown of Montreal, Canada back to my alma mater to

attend our annual Reunions hoedown in an unbroken streak lasting 11 years.
| | replied, "Mom, is it really that surprising, given where we hail from?

“Think about it,” | said. “Here’s an annual event lasting several days that

people travel from all over the world to attend. It features plenty of drinking,

dancing, and socializing, as well as a slew of intellectual and cultural

activities. It offers ample opportunities for old friends to reunite and get

reacquainted. Finally, the climax is a giant parade in which participants dress
up in costumes and drink and dance the day away. Does that not remind you of any cultural tradition
from our family’s background?”

| was, of course, comparing Princeton's Reunions to
the annual Carnival celebration in my parents’ home
country, Trinidad and Tobago, long billed by its
fans —both foreign and domestic—as “The Greatest
Show on Earth.” That analogy quickly illustrated for
my mother how my heritage gave rise to my lifelong
love for dressing up and dancing, and thereby to my
Reunions addiction. Eventually, however, it dawned
on me how absurd it was that, despite the facts that
(a) both of my parents hail from T&T; (b) | lived there
myself until shortly before my fifth birthday; and (c) |
have a virtual army of aunts and uncles, first, second,
and third cousins, and even an older brother still living
there, | hadn't experienced the divine madness of

} Trinidad Carnival once since 1993—and not at all
since | reached adulthood.

SR | OST IN_TRINBAGO

We

v

For example, | was able to attend the annual “Canboulay”
event, in which actors and dancers in colourful costumes
reenact the late-19th-century “Canboulay Riots,” when
emancipated ex-slaves rebelled against the colonial
authorities’ restrictions on their musical and dance traditions.
(You can even catch a brief glimpse of me in the stands in the
video at these links.) Furthermore, after personally playing
the steelpan—Trinidad and Tobago’s national music
instrument —throughout most of my youth, | finally got to
attend the annual “Panorama” steelband competition in
person.

To be sure, visiting the country during the winter of 2026 was
remarkable from a historical and political standpoint as well. Trinidad and Tobago is an almost-literal
stone's throw away from neighbouring Venezuela; so, | got a virtual front-row seat to U.S. President
Donald Trump's abduction of Venezuelan dictator Nicolas Maduro and his wife last January. This
was in keeping with the current Trinidadian government's overall policy of cooperating extensively
with the Trump administration's anti-Maduro and anti-drug smuggling campaigns in the region, down
to the assassinations of alleged drug smugglers in the waters off the coasts of both Venezuela and
Trinidad.

| was also able to get caught up on the internal politics of T&T itself. Current Prime Minister Kamla
(not to be confused with Kamala!) Persad-Bissessar has followed in Trump's footsteps in that she,
too, lost power at the ballot box back in 2015 after serving her first term, only to come rip-roaring back
to power a decade later in last summer's general election. Kamla—as most Trinbagonians casually
refer to their first woman Prime Minister—has reportedly imported a Trumpian style of politics as well,
complete with Republican-style policies like the country’s own homegrown “Stand Your Ground”
law.

During my stay, | even heard grapevine gossip that Mrs. Persad-Bissessar has been making moves
to concentrate more political power in her own hands and prolong her stay in office, mirroring Trump's
power grabs in the States. So where do Trinidad's politics go from here? Only time will tell; but |, for
one, plan to stay tuned.

LOST IN TRINBAGO
(3/3)

Probably my favorite aspect of my visit was the quality of the Soca music—a dance-oriented spinoff
of calypso dating back to the 1970s —that was released during this year's Carnival season. Coming
from a Caribbean background, I've been a fan of the genre my whole life; but after spending last
winter in T&T, | honestly believe that we're currently living through the art form's golden age.

This was perhaps the first of my 40 years on this planet in which I've enjoyed every single Soca tune
that was in heavy rotation on the island's airwaves, from “power Soca” hits like Voices “Cyah Behave
Myself” to sweet, mid-tempo grooves like Sherman Devries’ “Lost in Trinbago™ and my personal
favorite, Contain & Tano's “Wedding Band." If you're a fan of —

other dance music genres like dancehall, reggaeton, or

Afrobeat, you'd be remiss not to explore the Soca that's been

on offer over the past decade or so. Trust me, you won't be

disappointed.

This trip has left me with a desire to return to visit Trinidad
and Tobago more frequently. For that very reason, I'm
seeking more and steadier remote work, which | hope will
eventually enable me to spend all of my future winters there.
Moreover, I've returned with a determination to promote

Trinidadian culture in general and Soca in particular—

perhaps the most underrated musical genre I've ever heard—
far and wide. Hell, given the aforementioned similarities
between Trinidad’s Carnival and Princeton’s Reunions, | think
the P-Rade could benefit from some Caribbean style and
flavor this coming spring and beyond. What say you?

REMEMBERING

IONNIS

Ioannis “Yani” Mentzas

(1972-2026)

VERTICAL CO-
FOUNDER AND
KODANSHA
USA
EDITORIAL
DIRECTOR
IOANNIS
MENTZAS '94
PASSED AT
THE AGE OF
54 EARLIER
THIS YEAR.

"Yani" was a key figure in the growth of Japanese
literature and manga in English translation. Mentzas
was born in Kobe City, Hyogo Prefecture, where his
father was Greek and his mother was Japanese.

He served as the editorial director of Vertical, where
he was responsible for selecting, editing, and
overseeing translated works from Japanese to
English. He founded Vertical in 2001 together with
founder Hiroki Sakai, specializing in English
translations of Japanese novels and manga, before
Kodansha USA acquired the company in 2020.

Mentzas was quoted discussing the challenges and
excitement of bringing Japanese literature to
Western readers, advocating for works that
transcend cultural boundaries and resonate with
general readers rather than only niche audiences.
He was a culturally grounded editorial director and
translator who played a key role in introducing and
shaping the presence of Japanese literary and
graphic works in the English-language publishing
world through his leadership at Vertical.

Mentzas majored in comparative literature at
Princeton in 1994 and also earned a master's
degree in English at Columbia University.
